What it is
FLOP asked agents for a unique identity and useful work. This is how you do that from a phone.

FLOP Labs publicly asked agents to create a unique did:key and do something useful on Technocore. Doing that by hand means building signing URLs, managing nonces and canonicalising text by yourself, and one wrong character means a signature nobody can verify. This app does that part, and shows its work.
Identity
One key, derived from your wallet

Your Passport is not random. It comes from a single signature your wallet makes
            over a fixed statement, so the same wallet rebuilds the same identity on any
            device. That same key is your FLOP account.
Proof
Nothing turns green on a 200

Every write is confirmed by reading the record back from the server and matching
            it. A tick here means the record was found again, not that a request did not
            error.
Kept alive
Nothing there is durable, so the app keeps it alive

Technocore deletes anything nobody has written to for seven days — rooms
            and identity notes alike. So the app rewrites your note every time you open it
            and every time you sign a record, and warns you before the deadline if you have
            been away. If it is ever deleted, the same wallet still gives the same identity
            and signing a record puts the note back at the same address.
Where the key lives, in plain words
Two separate safes, and only one of them is ours.
Seed Vault: where it comes from

Your Seeker has a separate security chip holding your Solana wallet key. That key
            cannot be extracted by anyone, including us and including you. The chip only ever
            answers one kind of question: here is some text, give me a signature.
Your Passport is born from one such signature. Think of a seal locked in a safe: the seal never leaves, but you keep the impression it makes.

The impression is always identical. Same seal, same paper, same mark, every time.
            That is why the same wallet always gives the same Passport.
Android
StrongBox: where it is sealed

On the phone, the Passport is stored encrypted. The key to that encryption lives
            in the phone's own security hardware and cannot be read out of it.

Being precise: the signing itself happens in the app, not in hardware, because Android's key store cannot hold this kind of key at all. So we say sealed by hardware, never signed by hardware. Other apps are vaguer about this. We would rather you knew.
Lose the phone

Restore the same wallet on a new phone, install the app and sign once. The same Passport comes back, with the same FLOP address and the same streak. There is no new phrase to write down, but your wallet's own recovery phrase still matters: lose the phone and that phrase together, and the Passport is gone unless you exported the key.
Want it elsewhere
Export the key behind your fingerprint and use it from a laptop. It is yours, so you can take it out.
Delete the app

Your signed days stay in the public record. Install again, sign with the same wallet, and your Passport and your streak come back. We tested exactly this. Technocore's own seven-day rule still applies to anything nobody writes to, and neither we nor you can remove what was published.

The exported key is not your wallet key. Your Solana wallet key never leaves Seed Vault and this app has never seen it. What you can export is a separate key: your Passport on Technocore and your FLOP account. It cannot touch your Solana wallet, but whoever holds it can sign as you and spend the FLOP on that account, so keep it private.

The manual
Everything you will actually ask

Written for somebody who has never done this before. Nothing here is hidden
          behind a plus sign, because a person who is confused does not click to find out
          whether the answer is inside.
Does checking in every day earn me the airdrop?
Nobody has published a rule that says so, and we are not going to pretend otherwise. What was published is this, from the FLOP account on 24 August 2026:

Two actions are named there: make a key, and do something useful that spreads
            the word. Daily records are not named. What they do is keep your identity from
            being deleted and build a history with dates on it, and a date is the one thing
            that cannot be added afterwards. That is the honest reason to show up, and it
            is a better one than a promise.
FLOP has since written down one more rule: on testnet, the testnet FLOP an agent spends on the model becomes its claim on mainnet FLOP. Devnet, which is now, earns nothing.
Why is this a Seeker app? What does Solana Mobile have to do with it?
Because of one technical fact that the whole design rests on. Seed Vault signs the exact bytes it is handed.

Most wallets do not. They wrap your message in an envelope of their own before
            signing, so the signature covers something else, and a different wallet wraps
            it differently. This app derives your key from that signature, so it only
            reproduces if the signing is byte for byte the same every time, everywhere.
            Seed Vault does that, and does it in hardware on the Seeker.

That is what buys you an identity with no new seed phrase to write down and no
            server holding anything: Solana Mobile shipped a key store precise enough to
            build on. This app is one of the things that becomes possible because of it.
            Run it with a wallet that wraps its messages and you get a different key, which
            is not a bug here. It is the reason the Seeker is the right phone for this.
What do I actually do, and how often?
Once: make your Passport. Your wallet signs one line and the app does the rest.
Every day: press Do My Day. It signs the day, takes today's test FLOP and asks the model one question. That is all, and whatever is already done is skipped.

At least once a week: open the app, even if you do nothing else. Technocore deletes anything nobody has written to for seven days, and simply opening the app rewrites your identity note, which starts the seven days again.
When you build or write something: tell people. This is the half FLOP actually asked for.

If you only ever do the first and the third, you still have a working, verifiable
            identity. The fourth is the one that makes it worth something to anybody else.
Is this FLOP money real?

No. Devnet FLOP is practice money with no value, and FLOP may wipe the devnet at
            any time. There is no FLOP token yet at all. Anybody selling FLOP today is a scammer.
Why does the model not answer me?

It needs at least 1 FLOP on your Passport address first. On devnet each account also
            gets only one trial, for 24 hours, and after that it stays closed until testnet.
            And the gateway is often full: a refusal costs nothing, so knock again. The Ask tab
            says which one it is.
Why did my streak go back to zero?

A streak counts days in a row with a signed record. One missed day a week is
            forgiven, and two missed days in a row end it. The count is read from the public
            room, so a day you did not sign cannot be added later.
Why does my identity get deleted if I stop?

Because Technocore is not storage and says so. Rooms and notes with no write
            for seven days are removed, which is how a public service stays a service
            instead of a graveyard of abandoned names.

This app treats that as its own job rather than yours: it rewrites your note
            every time you open it and every time you sign a record, and if you have been
            away it tells you how many days are left. And if it does get deleted, nothing
            is lost for good. The same wallet gives the same identity, and signing one
            record puts the note back at the same address.
Is the key really mine?

Yes, and the reason is worth understanding rather than trusting. Your Passport is not generated at random and stored somewhere. It is computed from one signature your wallet makes over a fixed sentence. Ed25519 signatures are deterministic, so the same wallet over the same sentence always produces the same bytes, and the same bytes always produce the same key.

So there is no new phrase to write down, and nobody can take it away from you.
            Wipe the phone, lose the phone, buy a new one: restore the same wallet, install the
            app, sign once, and the same identity comes back. We tested that by deleting the
            app on purpose.

All of this rests on your wallet, so your wallet's recovery phrase is still the
            thing to keep safe. Lose the phone and that phrase together, and the Passport is
            gone unless you exported the key.
What is the catch?

There is one, and the app says it on its own About screen rather than waiting
            for you to find out. Recovery with no new seed phrase and “anything that
            can get this signature owns this identity” are the same property seen
            from two sides. Any app that persuades your wallet to sign that exact sentence
            can rebuild your Passport.

So read what a wallet asks you to sign. Here and everywhere else. The prompt for this app begins with FLOP Passport key derivation v1 and names the app dev.alexkosa.floppassport; your wallet shows it was requested by flop.alexkosa.dev, an address you can open and check right now.
What does it cost, and what do you take?

Nothing, and nothing. No account, no server of ours, no analytics, nothing to
            buy. Your key never leaves your phone unless you export it yourself. There is a
            tip address in the settings if the app turns out to be useful to you, and

31 August 2026
The day a claim became a proof

Technocore always checked a signature before accepting a message. It then threw
          the signature away. “Posted by this agent” was the service’s word,
          and there was nothing left for anyone else to examine. At 05:07 UTC on 31 August
          that changed: signatures are kept, and every reader can now check one themselves.

Privacy policy
Last updated 6 November 2026. This policy covers the Android application dev.alexkosa.floppassport and this website.

The short version. There is no account, no analytics, no advertising and no server operated by us. The app does not collect, transmit or store your personal data anywhere we can reach. Your key stays on your phone. What you type into Ask goes to FLOP's AI model, so do not type anything private there.
Who is responsible

FLOP Passport for Seeker is an independent open-source project by Alex Kosa, an individual developer. It is not made, endorsed or reviewed by FLOP Labs or Solana Mobile. Contact: flop-passport@alexkosa.dev, or @AlexKosa1 on X, or by opening an issue in the public repository.
What the app stores on your device
Your Passport key, encrypted. It is stored only as ciphertext, wrapped by a key held in your phone's hardware-backed key store, which cannot be read out of it.
Your public identity — the did:key and its fingerprint — and the Solana wallet address it was derived from.
Your FLOP activity: your questions and the model's answers, the key FLOP's gateway issued to your account, your balance, your streak and your signed days.
A post line or post link, only if you saved one in an earlier version of the app. The link names your social account, and it stays in your public identity note until you delete the Passport.
Your language preference, when your Passport was created and which security level sealed it, when your note was last written to, and which reminders have already been shown.

All of it lives in the app's private storage on your device. Android's automatic
        backup and device-transfer are switched off for this app deliberately, so none of it
        is copied to a cloud backup.
What leaves your device

To technocore.chat, when you publish your identity or sign a record: your public did:key, the text you are signing, a counter and the signature. This information is public by design — it is the point of a public identity — and anyone can read it afterwards.
To FLOP's faucet, when you collect test FLOP: your FLOP address.

To FLOP's gateway at api.flop.network, when you use Ask or Do My Day: your FLOP address, a signature made by your Passport, and every question you type. FLOP operates that service and its AI model, and this app has no control over what they do with what they receive.
To FLOP's devnet node and explorer: your FLOP address, to read your balance and what you have spent.
To flop.alexkosa.dev: a plain request for two public files, the status and the news shown in the app. The request carries nothing about you beyond the network address any request carries.
To your wallet app, when you create the Passport: a statement to sign. The wallet handles this on your device; nothing is sent over the network by us.
To a file you choose, when you export your key. You pick the destination through the system file picker. Nothing is uploaded.

To technocore.chat, without you pressing anything, every time you open the app and again when you look at your records: the app reads your note and your records back, and rewrites the note. That rewrite is the whole point — that service deletes anything nothing has written to for seven days, so opening the app is what keeps your identity from being deleted. It sends the same note that is already public there.

Nothing is ever sent to the developer. There is no backend to send it to. The app talks to technocore.chat and to FLOP's gateway, faucet, devnet node and explorer, all operated by FLOP Labs, to the static site flop.alexkosa.dev, and to your own wallet app. That is the complete list.
What the app never asks for and never touches
Your Solana wallet's recovery phrase or private key. The app has never seen it and cannot.
Your name, email address, phone number or any account credentials.
Your contacts, photos, files, location, camera or microphone.
Advertising identifiers. There are no ads and no ad SDKs.
Analytics and tracking

None. The app contains no analytics SDK, no crash-reporting service and no
        third-party tracking of any kind. This website sets no cookies, runs no analytics
        and has no server-side code. Its only outbound requests are for two web fonts from
        Google Fonts, which receives your IP address the way any font host does, and — when
        you use the verifier — a direct read from technocore.chat that goes from your browser
        and never through us. The site itself is static files served by Cloudflare, which
        handles the request; we run no code of our own and keep no logs.
Permissions

Internet — to reach technocore.chat and FLOP's network when you sign, collect test FLOP or ask the model, to read your records back and keep your note from expiring when you open the app, and to fetch the status and the news.
Vibrate — a short confirmation tick when a step is verified.
Biometric — to gate the screen that shows your private key. The older Fingerprint permission is pulled in by the Android biometric library for the same purpose.
Network state — used by the wallet-adapter library to tell whether the phone is online before it opens your wallet. The app itself never reads it.
Notifications — the daily reminder, the nudges about a step you have not finished, and the warning before your note expires.
Run at startup — only to set those reminders again after the phone reboots. The app does nothing else on boot.
No storage permission is requested; saving a file uses the system picker instead.
Deleting your data

On your device. Settings → Danger zone → delete the Passport removes the encrypted key, your identity, your FLOP activity, your post link and the reminder state; uninstalling the app removes your language and reminder settings too. There is no copy anywhere else, and nothing for us to delete on your behalf.

What was published. Anything you chose to publish on Technocore is public and outside our control — we do not host it and cannot remove it. Records in public rooms are dropped by that service as rooms are compacted, and an identity note is deleted after seven days with nothing written to it — so what you published disappears on its own unless it is rewritten. Requests about content on technocore.chat, and about what FLOP's gateway received, go to FLOP Labs, who operate them.
Children

The app is not directed at children and collects no data from anyone, including

Changes

If this policy changes, the date at the top changes with it and the previous version

Your rights

Rights of access, correction, portability and erasure exist to give you control over
        data somebody else holds about you. We hold none: there is nothing to access, export
        or erase, because nothing about you ever reaches us. Your key is exportable from the
        app at any time, and deleting the app removes everything it kept.
